precepts.text: Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, thou that leadest Joseph like a flock: this is Christ. Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh stir up thy strength, and come and save us. Turn us again: turn us again to your laws, turn us again to our identity, our nationality, and we shall be saved.
precepts.point: In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old.

note.label: Raising Up the Tabernacle of David That Fell

precepts.why:
Amos says, “I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old.” Asaph cries out for that raising: “Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, thou that leadest Joseph like a flock; thou that dwellest between the cherubims, shine forth.” The Shepherd of Israel is Christ.

“Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh stir up thy strength, and come and save us.” The tribes cry for him to stir up his strength and save them.

“Turn us again, O God, and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved.” Turn us again to your laws; turn us again to our identity, our nationality, and we shall be saved.

That is how the fallen tabernacle of David is rebuilt: the Shepherd of Israel turns the tribes back to his law and back to who they are, and closes up the breaches as in the days of old.

precepts.text: Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt; she sent out her boughs unto the sea.
precepts.point: His boughs, Israel, were delivered to death in the nether parts of the earth, and the nations shook at his fall.

note.label: The Kingdom Of Adam And The Old World

precepts.why:
Pharaoh is asked who he is like in his greatness, and the answer is the great cedar: “Behold, the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon with fair branches.” The Lord speaks to the prophets by similitudes, saying one thing that means another, and here he compares the Egyptian kingdom to Adam's kingdom, Adam ruling, to give us more insight into what we read in Genesis. “The waters made him great”: the waters that came from the Father made Adam great, flowing from him through all his plants, all Adam's children. And “his boughs were multiplied.” What are the boughs that multiplied?

Asaph answers in Psalm 80, crying to the “Shepherd of Israel, thou that leadest Joseph like a flock”: “Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it. Thou preparedst room before it, and didst cause it to take deep root, and it filled the land. The hills were covered with the shadow of it, and the boughs thereof were like the goodly cedars. She sent out her boughs unto the sea, and her branches unto the river.”

Those boughs are Israel, the sons of God. All of this is talking about Israel: all of us that were drinking that water, and everybody was not getting that water like us. Isaiah says the same: “In that day shall the branch of the Lord be beautiful and glorious.” The branches of the Lord are Israel, those of us that escape the destruction and get the kingdom.

So the boughs multiplied on the great cedar are Adam's true children, Israel, and the same vine the Lord brought out of Egypt and planted is the vine that filled the land with its shadow in Adam's kingdom.

precepts.text: The Lord gives the bread of adversity and the water of affliction.
precepts.point: Causing His face to shine goes into God having mercy on us, loving us, giving us strength, being on our behalf and fighting for us. It is like when Moses came down from the mountain and his face shone.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

precepts.why:
“Thou feedest them with the bread of tears; and givest them tears to drink in great measure.” The bread of tears goes into affliction, being afflicted because of our oppression. Isaiah speaks of the same meal: “And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity, and the water of affliction, yet shall not thy teachers be removed into a corner any more, but thine eyes shall see thy teachers”.

The Lord gives the bread of adversity and the water of affliction. That is the bread of tears and the tears to drink in great measure in Psalm 80, the Lord's anger against the prayer of his people, making us a strife unto our neighbours while our enemies laugh among themselves.

But the refrain follows: “Turn us again, O God of hosts, and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved.” Causing his face to shine goes into God having mercy on us, loving us, giving us strength, being on our behalf and fighting for us, like when Moses came down from the mountain and his face shone.

points: The prayer calls on the Shepherd of Israel that leads Joseph like a flock and dwells between the cherubims to shine forth before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: It asks Him to stir up His strength and come and save us, to turn us again and cause His face to shine that we shall be saved.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: It asks the Lord God of hosts how long He will be angry against the prayer of His people. He has fed them with the bread of tears and given them tears to drink in great measure.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: The bread of tears goes into affliction, being afflicted because of our oppression. Isaiah speaks of the Lord giving us the bread of adversity and the water of affliction.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: He has made us a strife unto our neighbors, and our enemies laugh among themselves. Again the refrain: turn us again, O God of hosts, and cause Thy face to shine, and we shall be saved.

Causing His face to shine goes into God having mercy on us, loving us, giving us strength, being on our behalf and fighting for us. It is like when Moses came down from the mountain and his face shone.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: The Most High brought a vine out of Egypt, cast out the heathen, and planted it. This is the israelites; we are that vine the Lord brought out of Egypt. He cast out the canaanites and planted us in Jerusalem and the land of Israel.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: He prepared room before it and caused it to take deep root, and it filled the land. This is how we grew as a nation.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: The hills were covered with the shadow of it, the boughs were like the goodly cedars, and she sent out her boughs unto the sea and her branches unto the river.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: Why then has He broken down her hedges, so that all they which pass by the way do pluck her? The "her" is Israel, that same vine brought out of Egypt.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: The boar out of the wood wastes it, and the wild beast of the field devours it.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: The plea is that the God of hosts return, look down from heaven, behold, and visit this vine and the vineyard which His right hand has planted, and the branch that He made strong for Himself.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: It is burned with fire and cut down; they perish at the rebuke of His countenance. His countenance is the face of God. When God came down in Exodus twenty, the people were in fear at His presence, not seeing His literal face but in fear because He is an omnipotent power.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: Let His hand be upon the man of His right hand, upon the son of man whom He made strong for Himself; so will we not go back from Him. Quicken us and we will call upon Thy name.

note.label: Psalm 80: The Vine Brought Out of Egypt

points: The closing refrain once more: turn us again, O Lord God of hosts, cause Thy face to shine, and we shall be saved. Causing His face to shine is Him taking us out of captivity and blessing us, the opposite of when He set His face against us.
